title: Mirabel and the Hymn
premise: Marguerite Iversen, a folklorist who hides behind his tape recorder and his skepticism, arrives in the isolated village of Hallowmere to document a funeral hymn the locals will sing once but never repeat. He discovers the hymn is a binding: each full performance feeds a presence called the Underchoir, which keeps the village's dead 'employed' in exchange for prosperity—and it has decided Marguerite's voice is the missing part of its final verse. As mirrors lag, then lie, then show him versions of himself that never happened, Marguerite must ally with the village's outcasts—the gravedigger's daughter Sef, and Old Wren, a woman the hymn failed to take—to learn the last verse without singing it. In the climax he performs the verse as pure recitation, breaking the contract at the cost of his own reflection, and chooses to stay in Hallowmere not as an observer but as family.
about_author: Astrid Okafor is the pen name of a former archivist of West African funeral songs who now writes horror from a farmhouse outside Bergen. Their work explores what communities bury in order to survive, and what refuses to stay buried.

chapters.title: The Song They Sing Once
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. He arrives in rain-soaked Hallowmere, charming the innkeeper into letting him record the harvest-eve hymn—once. The villagers' terror of repetition reads as quaint superstition. Emotional beat: smug professional detachment, undercut by a single wrong note in the recording that plays back even when the tape is stopped.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. At the inn, every mirror reflects him a beat late; by nightfall the reflection stops mimicking and simply watches. He blames exhaustion, alcohol, faulty silvering. Emotional beat: rationalist denial curdling into insomnia, as he catches his reflection mouthing words he hasn't said yet.

chapters.title: Sef of the Shallow Graves
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. The gravedigger's daughter, half-shunned for asking where the old graves went, finds Marguerite photographing headstones with no names. She trades information for escape money: the hymn has eleven verses, but no one alive knows the twelfth. Emotional beat: two lonely people recognizing each other's invisibility.

chapters.title: What the Village Buys
chapters.summary: Old Wren's POV. The oldest woman in Hallowmere, whom the hymn 'spat back,' explains the bargain: the Underchoir keeps crops fat and coffins light, paid in voices. Every singer loses a little of themselves until nothing remains but the song. Emotional beat: dread reframed as economics—justice was never part of the deal.

chapters.title: The Verse That Isn't Written
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Digging through parish records, he finds the hymn's composer erased from every document except one marginal sketch—a twelfth verse in notation no musician can read. His reflection begins singing it ahead of him. Emotional beat: obsession replacing skepticism; identity blurring as the mirror-version grows more confident than he is.

chapters.title: Harvest Eve
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV, rotating through villagers. The whole town sings verses one through ten while Marguerite secretly records; the fields visibly darken with each verse, fed like a mouth. A child goes missing afterward—the payment due. Emotional beat: complicity and guilt; Marguerite realizes his recording may have strengthened the thing.

chapters.title: The Missing Part
chapters.summary: Sef's POV. The missing child is found unharmed but voiceless, and the village turns on outsiders. Sef and Marguerite learn the truth: the Underchoir doesn't want a sacrifice—it wants a composer, someone to finish the verse and free it. It chose Marguerite because he listens. Emotional beat: horror of being wanted, of mattering for the worst reason.

chapters.title: Wren's Refusal
chapters.summary: Old Wren's POV. Wren reveals why the hymn rejected her: she once tried to sing the twelfth verse alone and lied about who she was, so it couldn't hold her. The verse can only be completed truthfully—by someone who says their own name and means it. Emotional beat: grief and defiance; she offers Marguerite her failure as a map.

chapters.title: The Eleventh Hour
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. On the winter solstice the mirrors fail entirely, and the Underchoir speaks through them directly, offering him everything he's fled: recognition, belonging, a name that echoes. His reflection steps out to sing in his place. Emotional beat: temptation at its most intimate—he must refuse the self he could become.

chapters.title: Sung Once, Never Twice
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, closing with Sef's. He recites the twelfth verse—spoken, never sung, his true name given freely—and the mirrors shatter, the hymn dies mid-note, and the village wakes poorer but free. He stays, taking a room above Sef's kitchen. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; found family, justice rendered outside any law, and a man finally visible on his own terms.
